title: In orbit, an astronaut’s weight-bearing bones lose 1–1.5% of their density each month

cover.alt: An astronaut on the space station runs on a treadmill, held down by a white harness clipped to a bungee cord, with racks of equipment around him.

body: On Earth, the bones of your hips and legs carry your weight with every step. In orbit there is no weight to carry, and NASA says **weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month**, while muscles waste faster than they would on the ground. So crews on the International Space Station typically exercise for about two hours a day: they run on a treadmill with a harness and bungee cords pulling them down onto the belt, pedal a fixed bike and lift against a resistance machine. Even so, NASA says some of the lost bone might not be fully restored after landing, although astronauts’ risk of fractures is not higher.

slides.alt: A montage aboard the space station: an astronaut in a harness runs on a treadmill, tethered to it by white bungee cords; another works out standing on an exercise machine; one pedals a fixed bike while wearing a headset; another runs on the treadmill in a harness.
slides.caption: Aboard the space station, astronauts run on a treadmill strapped down by a harness and bungee cords, and work out on a fixed bike and other exercise machines.

slides.prompt: Why does a runner on the space station’s treadmill wear a harness clipped to bungee cords?
slides.answer: To pull them down onto the belt
slides.detail: With nothing holding them down, the first push of a foot would send them floating off the treadmill. The cords stand in for their missing weight.

slides.label: of their mineral density lost each month by weight-bearing bones in space
slides.text: Typical space station missions last six to 12 months, so the losses add up.

slides.heading: Of every 24 hours on the space station, about two go on exercise
slides.note: Running, cycling and resistance training, most days

slides.heading: How NASA fights bone and muscle loss
items: A good diet, to limit muscle loss
Bisphosphonate drugs, which NASA studies found prevent bone loss

slides.question: Which bones lose density fastest in orbit?
options: The small bones of the hands
slides.explanation: Bones that carry your weight on Earth, such as those of the hips and legs, lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density a month during spaceflight.

source.label: NASA: The Human Body in Space
